VIABILITY: The model has a credible, fundable path to revenue. Two paying customers ($15,500 booked) from a student-run pilot is meaningful early validation, and the pain point (inaccurate, late, low-response commute surveys, with commuting often 20-40% of Scope 3) was corroborated by eleven officer interviews. Pricing is sensible: the $6,000 minimum fee and $9,500 advisory package undercut the $15,000-$40,000 consulting surveys, and funding sources (sustainability budgets, parking revenue, green fees) are realistic. Bundling measurement with behavior change is a differentiated wedge, and a free consumer app removes end-user payment friction. The $25,000 ask is modest and its allocation (product hardening, conversion of warm leads, legal review) is coherent and proportionate.

KEY ASSUMPTION WEAKNESSES: (1) Market sizing is internally shaky. $4.50 x commuters x 1,100 campuses = $38M implies about 7.7M commuters (~7,700 per campus), which is plausible only if 40% of enrollment commutes AND every enrolled commuter is billed. But pricing per enrolled commuter conflicts with the revenue reality: the pilot reached only 11% adoption. If billing is per app user, revenue per campus is roughly 4-9x lower than the headline TAM implies; if per eligible commuter, universities will balk at paying for non-users. This pricing-basis ambiguity is the single biggest hole in the model. The $200M+ expansion to hospitals and employers is speculative and unvalidated; those buyers have different needs and incumbents. (2) The pilot license ($6,000) is just the minimum fee, so it provides no evidence of per-commuter price acceptance. With 1,840 users at $3-5, the license would exceed $6,000, suggesting the university paid the floor, not the formula. (3) The 14% reduction in solo trips is promising but comes from a self-selected, opted-in 11% over 12 weeks, with likely selection bias and unproven persistence; the 21 tonnes figure is estimated, not verified. Institutions will need to extrapolate this to the other 89% who did not enroll. (4) Data/measurement validity: aggregate dashboards from 10-20% adoption raise representativeness concerns, precisely the weakness of surveys the product claims to fix. Self-selected app users skew toward the engaged and the young, and the company must show weighting or validation methods to be credible for formal climate reporting. (5) CAC of $4,000 recovered in year one looks optimistic given higher-ed sales cycles (often 6-18 months, committee and procurement/IT security reviews, FERPA and privacy scrutiny for location tracking). Only two sales so far, both warm relationships. (6) Financial projections (eight campuses and $190K in year two, 25 campuses and $720K in year three) imply roughly $23K-29K average revenue per campus, which is plausible only with advisory attach and meaningful per-commuter fees; it is aggressive relative to a $6,000-$15,500 observed ACV. Breakeven in year three with two engineers, an analyst and cloud costs seems feasible but leaves no budget for sales hiring, which will be required beyond the local beachhead.

SCALABILITY: Software licensing at 78% gross margin is scalable, and the data flywheel claim (mode-detection and intervention-effect models improving with each campus) is reasonable but not yet a moat; larger players (corporate commute platforms, mobility data firms, Google/Apple location APIs, transit agency tools) could add campus modules. The advisory stream (55% margin, in-person, regional) scales linearly with headcount and travel, so it is useful for landing accounts but will cap growth if it remains the main motion. The 140-campus beachhead is sensible for cost-effective in-person selling, but the jump to 1,100 campuses needs a lower-touch, repeatable sales motion, which the plan acknowledges as a goal but has not demonstrated. Technical scalability concerns: battery drain, mode-detection accuracy across diverse geographies, iOS/Android background-location policy changes, and privacy regimes (state laws, GDPR-like consent) are ongoing operating risks. Seasonality (semester cycles, annual budgeting) and churn if campuses see it as a one-time inventory exercise are also risks; the recurring value proposition (annual reporting plus intervention tracking) must be proven.

TEAM AND EXECUTION: The team is well matched (economics/sustainability funding experience, a shipped location-feature engineer, transit-planning partnerships, faculty advisor with inventory experience), but all are students with graduation timing risk and no enterprise or higher-ed sales veteran.

BOTTOM LINE: Moderately strong early-stage venture with real pain, early revenue and a plausible differentiated product, but the headline TAM and per-commuter economics are overstated relative to observed adoption and pricing evidence. Viability in the regional niche is good; scalability to a national, venture-scale business depends on clarifying the pricing basis, proving data representativeness at low adoption rates, shortening and standardizing the sales cycle, and defending against feature-level competition. Recommended next steps: sign the six warm campuses at the formula price (not the minimum), validate persistence of behavior change over a full academic year, and publish a methodology for weighting app data against census-style commuter counts.

Business plan text:

Greenlight Commute
Greenlight Commute: Executive Summary
The Problem
Universities are under rising pressure to measure and reduce their carbon footprints, yet most
cannot say how much of that footprint comes from the way their own people get to campus.
Commuting is typically the largest single component of a campus's Scope 3 emissions; in
published campus inventories it commonly accounts for 20 to 40 percent of total emissions, and
at commuter-heavy schools more. It is also the component hardest to measure.
The standard tool is an annual travel survey. Our interviews with eleven sustainability
officers at institutions in our region confirmed what the literature suggests: response rates
average 8 to 15 percent, answers describe a single typical day rather than actual behavior, and
results arrive months late. One officer told us her office reports a commuting figure "we know
is wrong but can't improve." Meanwhile, more than 1,100 US campuses have signed public climate
commitments with reporting obligations, and the offices responsible are typically staffed by
one to three people with no data engineers.
The Solution
Greenlight Commute is a mobile app paired with an advisory service.
For commuters, the app, used with opt-in consent, logs trips to and from campus, identifies the
travel mode, and estimates the emissions of each trip. It then shows each user a personalized
"switch plan": for example, replacing three of five weekly solo drives with a bus route that
adds nine minutes to the trip and saves 11.4 kilograms of carbon dioxide per week. It matches
carpool partners among enrolled users, surfaces transit and bike-share options, and gives
modest rewards, such as campus-store credits funded by the university, for sustained mode
shifts.
For sustainability offices, we provide an anonymized, aggregated dashboard showing emissions by
mode, by origin zone and by population group, plus an annual advisory report formatted for
climate-action reporting and a set of targeted intervention recommendations, such as where a
new shuttle stop would remove the most solo-driving trips. Individual data is never shared with
the institution. Location data is aggregated before leaving our servers, and users can delete
their history at any time.
The distinctive element is that we deliver measurement and behavior change together. Survey
vendors measure but do not change behavior; consumer carbon apps change behavior but give
institutions no usable data. Our pilot shows the combination works.
Market
There are roughly 3,900 degree-granting institutions in the United States enrolling about 19
million students and employing several million faculty and staff. We focus first on the roughly
1,100 campuses with public climate commitments and a dedicated sustainability office. At our
target price of $4.50 per enrolled commuter per year, and assuming 40 percent of enrolled
populations commute, serving these campuses represents a serviceable market of about $38
million annually. Adding advisory work and extending to hospitals and large employers, which
face similar reporting pressure, raises the opportunity above $200 million. Our initial
beachhead is the 140 campuses within a day's travel of our university, where in-person advisory
is cost-effective.
Business Model
Revenue comes from two streams. The first is an annual software license priced per enrolled
commuter, ranging from $3.00 to $5.00 depending on volume, with a minimum annual fee of $6,000.
The second is advisory services: the annual report and intervention analysis at $9,500 for a

standard package, and custom studies for transit-planning projects at $15,000 to $30,000.
Universities can fund these from sustainability budgets, parking and transportation revenue, or
green-fee funds, which several campuses already administer for exactly this purpose. Our
commuter-facing app is free, so adoption is not constrained by individual willingness to pay.
We estimate gross margin at 78 percent for licenses and 55 percent for advisory work, and a
customer acquisition cost of about $4,000 per campus, recovered within the first contract year.
Competition
Campus transportation surveys offered by consulting firms are slow, costly at $15,000 to
$40,000 per cycle, and low in response. Corporate commute-management platforms focus on parking
and employee benefits rather than emissions reporting, and do not serve student populations.
Consumer carbon-footprint apps lack institutional dashboards and rely on self-reported trips.
Transit agencies collect ridership data but nothing on trips they do not carry. No competitor
we found combines passive trip measurement, behavior-change recommendations and reporting
designed for campus climate commitments. Our advantage is reinforced by our data: each enrolled
campus improves our mode-detection accuracy and our estimates of the impact of each type of
intervention.
Team
Priya Raghunathan, chief executive, is a senior in environmental economics who managed our
university's student sustainability fund and led the commuter-survey redesign that raised
campus response from 11 to 19 percent. Marcus Delacroix-Whitfield, chief technology officer, is
a computer science senior who built the trip-detection engine and previously interned on a
mobile data team, shipping a location-based feature used by 200,000 people. Tomasz OkonkwoNowak, head of partnerships, is a master's student in urban planning who spent two years
working with the regional transit authority on service-gap analysis. Our faculty advisor in the
sustainability institute has overseen three campus emissions inventories.
Milestones and Financials
We have formed Greenlight Commute LLC and defined the core product concept and data model. Our
pilot on our own campus enrolled 1,840 commuters over one semester, 11 percent of the commuting
population, and signed two paid agreements: a $6,000 annual license with our university's
sustainability office and a $9,500 advisory engagement with a neighboring college. Among pilot
participants who received switch plans, solo-driving trips fell 14 percent relative to a
matched group over twelve weeks, avoiding an estimated 21 metric tons of carbon dioxide. Early
projections: $15,500 in booked revenue this year, rising to $190,000 in year two with eight
campuses and $720,000 in year three with twenty-five. We expect to reach breakeven during year
three, with costs driven mainly by two engineers, a part-time analyst and cloud infrastructure.
What We Ask For
We are seeking a $25,000 prize or seed grant to fund our next twelve months: roughly $12,000 to
harden the app's trip detection and privacy architecture, $8,000 to convert six campuses now in
conversation from pilot discussions to signed contracts, and $5,000 for legal review of dataprotection agreements. We would also value introductions to campus sustainability networks and
mentorship from judges experienced in selling to higher education. With this support, we will
have eight paying campuses and a repeatable sales process by the end of next year.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.
